questions.text: What is a meaningful part of a large information system called?
questions.explanation:
A subsystem is one part of a larger system with a defined responsibility.

Why the answer fits: It identifies the correct concept rather than a nearby but different activity.

Example: Registration is one part of a student management system.

Student note: It is not automatically the same as one source-code function.

questions.text: CampCart is a small online grocery service for registered college residents. A Customer signs in, browses available items, and adds any quantity within stock limits to a Cart. During checkout the system calculates the amount, receives a delivery address, requests payment authorization, and creates an Order only when payment succeeds. The system reduces stock, sends the order to the store and notifies the Customer. Declined payment leaves the cart unchanged. An administrator maintains item information and views order reports. Fill the four-row classification table. The rows must appear in this order: 1) customer need, 2) a system function, 3) expected business benefit, 4) a detailed implementation choice. For each row type the matching category (Problem / Capability / Benefit / Design detail) and the short tag from this word bank: stock errors / checkout / fewer failed orders / database indexing.
questions.correctAnswer:
1 Problem | stock errors
2 Capability | checkout
3 Benefit | fewer failed orders
4 Design detail | database indexing
questions.explanation:
A vision starts with the need, then identifies high-level capabilities and expected benefits. Implementation detail is usually deferred.

1. Read the purpose of each row.
2. Select the matching category and short tag from the word bank.

Example: Checkout is a capability, not a problem.

Student note: The table tests classification, not the ability to memorise a long paragraph. Each correct expected cell earns a share of the mark.

study.title: System vision classification
study.simple: A high-level system vision states the problem, relevant capabilities and expected value. Database-level details belong in later design.
steps: Separate the problem from the function meant to solve it.
Separate business benefit from detailed design choices.
study.example: Checkout is a system capability; fewer failed orders is a benefit.
study.pitfall: Avoid classifying how something is implemented as the customer problem.

keyTerms.meaning: Short high-level summary of why and what the planned system should do.

questions.text: ToolTrade helps local makers borrow equipment. A registered Member may advertise several Tools with an identifier, condition and availability. Another Member creates a Rental for one listed Tool, with start/end dates and a status. Each Rental has one borrower, one Tool and may record one or more Payment attempts. An Owner is a Member whose tool is listed. A returned Tool may receive a Rating linked to its Rental. Draw a UML domain class diagram with important classes, identifying attributes, labelled associations and realistic multiplicities.
questions.correctAnswer: Member(memberId,name) 1 owner to 0..* Tool(toolId,condition,available), Member 1 borrower to 0..* Rental(rentalId,start,end,status), Rental 1 to 1 Tool, Rental 1 to 0..* Payment(paymentId,amount,status), Rental 1 to 0..1 Rating(score,comment). One Tool may participate in many Rentals across time, but each Rental references one Tool.
aiRubric: Owner vs borrower roles of Member
No UI/controller classes mixed into a domain model
questions.aiReferenceNotes: Model domain nouns as classes, then add attributes and associations with realistic multiplicities. Identify Member, Tool, Rental and supporting concepts. Add key fields and important business attributes. Connect owner, borrower, rental, payment and optional rating roles. Distinguish a person's two roles; do not duplicate the same Member data unless there is a sound reason.
questions.explanation:
Model domain nouns as classes, then add attributes and associations with realistic multiplicities.

Method:
1. Identify Member, Tool, Rental and supporting concepts.
2. Add key fields and important business attributes.
3. Connect owner, borrower, rental, payment and optional rating roles.

Example: A maker can own many tools, and one tool can have several rentals across different dates.

Student note: Distinguish a person's two roles; do not duplicate the same Member data unless there is a sound reason.
